title: Most Profit Assigning Work
description: Maximize total profit assigning workers to jobs they qualify for, using a sort-both-sides two-pointer sweep tracking the best unlocked profit.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Given parallel arrays difficulty and profit describing jobs, and an array worker giving each worker's ability, a worker can do a job if their ability is at least that job's difficulty. Each worker takes at most one job (a job can be done by multiple workers, or none), earning that job's profit. Every worker picks the best job they qualify for. Return the maximum total profit across all workers.

blocks.caption: Sorting both jobs and workers lets a single sweep track the best profit unlocked so far.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","difficulty[], profit[] (parallel, one entry per job), worker[] (one ability per worker)"],["Rule","A worker can take any job with difficulty at or below their ability, earning its profit"],["Output","Maximum total profit summed over all workers, each choosing their single best qualifying job"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

Since a worker with a given ability can take ANY job at or below that difficulty (not just the closest one), what matters is the BEST profit among all jobs unlocked so far, not the profit of the job matching that exact difficulty. Sorting both jobs (by difficulty) and workers (by ability) lets a two-pointer sweep track this running best in a single pass.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: This "sort both sides, sweep together tracking a running best" technique reapplies whenever a threshold-based eligibility (here, ability >= difficulty) determines access to a value that should be maximized, not matched exactly.
3. Understand the Problem

Picture workers lining up from weakest to strongest ability. As weaker workers are processed first, only easier jobs are unlocked; as the line progresses to stronger workers, more (harder) jobs become unlocked too. At each point, every worker in line should take the BEST-PAYING job unlocked so far, not necessarily the hardest one, since an easier job might actually pay more.

blocks.caption: Every worker takes the best-paying job unlocked by their ability level so far.

items: Sort jobs by difficulty, and workers by ability.
Sweep both lists together: as a worker's ability unlocks more jobs (difficulty <= ability), track the running best profit among all unlocked jobs.
Each worker earns that running best profit; sum across all workers for the total.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
difficulty = [2,4,6,8,10], profit = [10,20,30,40,50], worker = [4,5,6,7]. Jobs sorted by difficulty (already sorted here), workers sorted: [4,5,6,7].

blocks.content: {"headers":["Worker ability","Jobs newly unlocked (difficulty <= ability)","Best profit so far","Worker earns"],"rows":[["4","(2,10), (4,20)","20","20"],["5","none new","20","20"],["6","(6,30)","30","30"],["7","none new","30","30"]]}

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: Total profit = 20 + 20 + 30 + 30 = 100, matching the expected output. Job (10,50) is never unlocked since no worker has ability 10 or higher.
5. How Should We Think?
A direct approach checks every worker against every job, tracking the best profit among all jobs that worker qualifies for. This is correct but rechecks all jobs for every worker.

Sorting both jobs and workers lets a two-pointer sweep process everything in a single combined pass: as workers are processed in increasing ability order, the job pointer only ever moves FORWARD, since a stronger worker unlocks a superset of what a weaker worker unlocked, letting the running best-profit-so-far carry over directly.
6. Brute Force Solution
For each worker, scan all jobs to find the best profit among those they qualify for.
7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n * m)","n workers, m jobs, every worker scans every job"],["Space","O(1)","No extra storage beyond the running total"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Rescanning all jobs for every worker is unnecessary once sorting lets the "best unlocked profit so far" carry forward between workers.
8. Optimize the Solution

Sort jobs by difficulty and workers by ability. Sweep workers in increasing ability order; for each worker, advance the job pointer through all jobs now unlocked (difficulty <= this worker's ability), updating the running best profit. Add that running best to the total for each worker.

items: Sort jobs by difficulty and workers by ability, O(n log n + m log m).
Two-pointer sweep: advance the job pointer only forward, updating the running best profit as new jobs unlock.
Sum the running best profit once per worker.

blocks.text: 9. Optimized Solution

codes.python:
def max_profit_assignment(difficulty, profit, worker):
    jobs = sorted(zip(difficulty, profit))
    sorted_workers = sorted(worker)

    i = 0
    best = 0
    total = 0
    n = len(jobs)

    for ability in sorted_workers:
        while i < n and jobs[i][0] <= ability:
            best = max(best, jobs[i][1])
            i += 1
        total += best

    return total


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(max_profit_assignment([2, 4, 6, 8, 10], [10, 20, 30, 40, 50], [4, 5, 6, 7]))
    print(max_profit_assignment([85, 47, 57], [24, 66, 99], [40, 25, 25]))

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space"],"rows":[["Brute Force, scan all jobs per worker","O(n * m)","O(1)"],["Optimized, sort + two-pointer sweep","O(n log n + m log m)","O(n + m)"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: When eligibility is threshold-based (ability >= difficulty) and the goal is the BEST value unlocked (not the matching one), track a running maximum as the threshold advances.
Sorting both sides of a threshold relationship lets a two-pointer sweep process everything in one combined linear pass after the sort.
The running best-so-far never needs to decrease as the threshold advances, since anything unlocked earlier remains unlocked later.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

Most Profit Assigning Work is solved by sorting jobs by difficulty and workers by ability, then sweeping both together with a running "best profit unlocked so far" that only ever grows as more jobs become accessible. Each worker earns that running best, giving an O(n log n + m log m) solution instead of checking every worker against every job.
